subject: Biology
title: Antibiotics: Discovery and Use
description: A quick win: understand Antibiotics: Discovery and Use.

hook.text: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed mold killing bacteria on a forgotten petri dish.

buildup.text: The mold was Penicillium, and the substance it released—penicillin—became the first antibiotic.

discovery.text: Antibiotics work by targeting bacterial processes: cell walls, protein synthesis, or DNA copying.

twist.text: Antibiotics don't work on viruses at all—yet they are overprescribed for viral infections.

climax.text: Since Fleming's accident, antibiotics have saved an estimated 200 million lives.

punchline.text: A forgotten dish saved 200 million lives.

quiz.question: Why don't antibiotics work against viruses?
options: Viruses lack the cellular structures antibiotics target
Viruses are too small for drugs to reach
Antibiotics destroy all types of microbes equally

details.summary: Alexander Fleming's 1928 discovery of penicillin launched the antibiotic revolution that transformed medicine. Antibiotics kill bacteria or inhibit their growth by targeting cell walls, protein synthesis, or DNA replication, saving hundreds of millions of lives over the past century.
details.whyItMatters: Antibiotics are among the most important medical discoveries in history. They made modern surgery, organ transplants, and cancer chemotherapy possible by preventing bacterial infections that would otherwise be fatal.
takeaways: Fleming discovered penicillin from a Penicillium mold contaminating a bacterial plate
Antibiotics target bacterial structures and processes absent in human cells
The golden age of antibiotic discovery occurred from the 1940s to 1960s

faq.question: How did Alexander Fleming discover penicillin?
faq.answer: Fleming noticed a mold contaminating a bacterial culture plate had killed surrounding bacteria. He identified the mold as Penicillium and the antibacterial substance as penicillin. Florey and Chain later developed mass production methods that saved millions in World War II.

faq.question: Why do antibiotics work on bacteria but not viruses?
faq.answer: Antibiotics target structures unique to bacteria like cell walls, bacterial ribosomes, and bacterial enzymes. Viruses lack these structures because they hijack host cell machinery. Antivirals must target viral-specific processes, which is why they are harder to develop.
